Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In an analysis published on April 16, 2024, it was reported that U.S. dairy exports showed positive growth in February 2024 for the first time in a year. This recovery was largely attributed to a significant 32.1% year-on-year increase in cheese exports, which grew by over 10,000 tons. The surge in export activity was likely supported by lower average unit prices for most major dairy products. Specifically, the average unit price for cheese was $4.56/kg, a 15% decrease from the previous year. <2> An analysis published on March 18, 2024, concluded that continued weak demand for cheese and nonfat dry milk (NDM) was the primary factor suppressing milk prices, despite a tightening milk supply in the U.S. and globally. The report also highlighted a worsening income-over-feed-cost (IOFC) outlook for dairy producers. This margin squeeze was attributed to lower Class III futures, which had dropped nearly $1 per hundredweight (cwt) compared to the previous month, combined with slightly increased feed costs for corn and soybean meal. Additionally, the analysis noted that a smaller supply of dairy animals had led to a rise in the value of replacement heifers. <3> The USDA's Agricultural Prices report for January 2024 indicated that the all-milk price was $20.10 per hundredweight (cwt). [1, 2] This represents a decrease of $0.50 from December 2023 and is $3.00 lower than the price in January 2023. [1, 2] Additionally, the USDA's dairy index for January experienced a 2.4% decline compared to the previous month. [1] <4> A market analysis for February 2024 revealed a mixed outlook for the dairy industry. While there was some improvement in overall milk prices, Class III futures for February and March were projected to stay below $17/cwt. A significant mitigating factor for producers was the substantial decline in feed costs, with corn and soybean meal futures approaching their contract lows. Furthermore, the U.S. dairy heifer inventory had fallen to its lowest level since 2004, a key detail suggesting that any potential for herd expansion would be significantly constrained. <5> A report from the U.S. Dairy Export Council (USDEC) shows that U.S. dairy export volume declined by 7% in 2023 compared to the record-setting year of 2022. The total export value for 2023 was $8.11 billion, a 16% decrease from the previous year, though it still ranks as the second-highest value on record. Key factors contributing to this decline included elevated inflation, slower economic growth, and soft demand in key markets, particularly China. Additionally, increased competition from other major exporters like the EU and New Zealand impacted U.S. performance. While most major product categories saw a downturn, high-protein whey and lactose exports experienced volume gains of 18% and 5% respectively. <6> A mid-January market update highlighted significant financial strain on dairy producers, citing low Class III milk prices. [5] As of January 16, 2024, futures for the first quarter of the year averaged just $15.69 per hundredweight (cwt), a level considered unsustainable for many farmers. [5] The report noted that despite lagging milk production in the United States and internationally, prices had not increased, indicating subdued consumer demand. [5] This weak demand was attributed to the global impact of inflation and other macroeconomic factors on consumers. [5] <7> The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) program made payments to enrolled dairy producers for all months in 2023 except November, due to low margins caused by high feed costs and low milk prices. [5] The income over feed margin for October 2023 was announced as $9.44 per hundredweight (cwt), triggering payments for producers with coverage levels of $9.50. [3, 5] This continued a trend of rising margins from a low point earlier in the year, with the August margin at $6.46 per cwt and September at $8.44 per cwt. [5] The USDA announced the October margin details on November 30, 2023. [3] By the end of September 2023, the DMC program had disbursed over $1.27 billion in indemnity payments for the year. [7] Roughly 17,085 dairy operations, accounting for about 80% of all U.S. dairies, were enrolled in the program for 2023. [5] <8> On October 11, 2023, Ben Laine, an economist with Terrain, reported a shift in the primary driver of milk price volatility from supply levels to consumer demand. [1] Laine stated that while domestic demand for dairy remains strong, fluctuations are increasingly influenced by unstable international markets. [1] He further explained that a surge in milk production from the European Union has competitively priced the U.S. out of some export markets. [1] <9> In a campaign launched by the animal rights organization PETA, actor James Cromwell starred in a satirical video released on September 28, 2023, just ahead of National Coffee Day. [1, 3] In the video, his first acting role since the series *Succession*, Cromwell portrays a fictional, greedy Starbucks executive who extols the company's practice of applying a surcharge for vegan milk options. [2, 3] The video splices Cromwell's performance with imagery of industrial dairy farming, calves being separated from their mothers, and scenes of environmental damage like melting ice caps and wildfires. [3] The fictional executive explains that while Starbucks is aware of the dairy industry's negative impact, they charge extra for plant-based milks because they know conscientious consumers are willing to pay more. [1, 2] This video was part of a broader PETA campaign featuring Cromwell to protest Starbucks' vegan milk upcharge, which has also included other forms of protest. [4, 7] For instance, in May 2022, Cromwell glued his hand to a Starbucks counter in New York City. [7, 10] Another component of the campaign in May 2023 involved displaying Cromwell's face on nearly 100 screens along the Atlantic City Boardwalk with a message urging Starbucks to end the surcharge. [4, 5]

[1, 5] In the 24 major producing states, production was 18.8 billion pounds, a 3.5% increase from the prior year. [2] The number of milk cows in these states rose by 154,000 head to 9.04 million, with the average production per cow at 2,081 pounds, up by 36 pounds. [1, 5] The USDA also revised the June 2024 production increase to be 3.4%. [3] <8> A dairy market analysis dated July 16, 2025, indicated a significant squeeze on farmer margins due to rising feed costs while milk prices remained stagnant. This situation pushed the milk-to-feed ratio down to 1.8, a low point in the 25th percentile for July. However, the report highlighted a risk management opportunity, with Q4 Class III futures trading at $17.90, nearly a full dollar above the cash market. This premium offered a potential $10,000 in extra monthly revenue for a farm shipping one million pounds. On a global scale, the analysis noted a positive development: U.S. nonfat dry milk (NDM) became price-competitive for the first time in the year, priced at $2,822/MT against Europe's $2,750/MT for SMP. <9> A global surge in milk prices is being driven by soaring temperatures and heightened humidity, which cause heat stress in cows and lead to reduced milk production. [1, 6] Scientists warn that extreme heat can reduce milk production by up to 10%, and if high temperatures persist for more than a week, these losses can exceed 25%. [6, 8] The effects of heat stress on milk production can linger for more than 10 days after a hot spell. [6, 8] This phenomenon threatens the long-term sustainability of the dairy industry, which is already dealing with other climate-related challenges and the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. [6, 7] While modern cooling systems like fans and water sprayers can mitigate some losses, their effectiveness diminishes as temperatures continue to rise. [6, 8] Many farms, particularly in hotter climates, cannot afford such technologies, making the global dairy industry vulnerable to the increasing frequency of heatwaves. [6] Experts are calling for systemic changes, including rethinking agricultural policies and breeding more heat-resistant cow varieties to ensure future food security. The overall 2025 all-milk price forecast was increased by five cents to $22.00 per cwt. Looking ahead to 2026, the USDA projects a further increase in milk production to 229.1 billion pounds, with a forecasted Class III price of $17.85 per cwt and a Class IV price of $18.60 per cwt.
